newsitem.title: USA: Deadly turkey disease cuts flocks in N. Carolina.
newsitem.headline: Deadly turkey disease cuts flocks in N. Carolina.

text.p: Scientists are working feverishly to find a cure for a mysterious disease that killed millions of young turkeys in North Carolina since 1995, but they expect it to kill millions more this spring and summer.

"We are working from a research standpoint that the disease is going to come back and it's going to be just as severe as last year," said Oscar Fletcher, dean of North Carolina State University's College of Veterinary Medicine.
The disease is Poult Enteritis Mortality Syndrome (PEMS). It attacks young turkeys and 50 percent or more of infected birds die. The survivors are left weakened and in poor health.

Fletcher was not optimistic a cure will be found soon. Scientists have yet to isolate the cause, although they suspect a virus, he said. Discovered in 1991 in Union County, N.C., turkey flocks. The disease spread throughout the southern North Carolina and into other southern states.
"I just don't believe we will have a magic answer between now and May," he said.

North Carolina is the leading U.S. turkey state, producing about 59.5 million birds in 1996. The state lost about two million turkeys to the disease each year in 1995 and 1996, said Joel Brandenberger, National Turkey Federation spokesman.

The deaths have not affected national turkey production, which hit a record-high 297 million birds in 1996. Also, the disease is not harmful to humans and is not believed to be contagious to other poultry species.
"It has not taken a toll on the industry's overall production," Brandenberger said.
The disease appears in mid-May and flourishes in warm weather, attacking young turkeys about a month after birth.
"One of the problems is, even the birds that survive don't do very well," said John Atwell, director of a North Carolina Department of Agriculture animal disease laboratory.
Last month, WLR Foods Inc, a huge southeast turkey and chicken processor, said it was cutting production at 45 of its 151 farms in an attempt to curb the spread of the disease.
"If we continue with this poult (young turkeys) suspension, we will be down 10 percent in production," said Gail Price, spokeswoman for WLR Foods Inc.
North Carolina State's Fletcher supported WLR Foods' action, noting that reducing the turkey population may control spread of the disease.
